genocide.definition: The deliberate killing of a large number of people from a particular nation or ethnic group with the aim of destroying that nation or group.
genocide.extendedDefinition: As defined by the 1948 UN Convention, genocide includes acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group. The word was coined in 1944 by the jurist Raphael Lemkin, who combined the Greek genos (people) with the Latin -cide (killing) to name what Churchill had called "a crime without a name."

massHomicide.definition: The umbrella construct proposed by Dutton, Boyanowsky & Bond (2005) for all large-scale, intentional, group-perpetrated killing of defenseless people.
massHomicide.extendedDefinition: The term deliberately spans events usually studied separately — military massacres, genocides, and political slaughters — so that their shared psychological and organizational mechanisms can be compared within a single framework.

massacre.definition: The deliberate and indiscriminate killing of a large number of defenseless people, typically localized and completed within hours or days.
massacre.extendedDefinition: Massacres usually erupt inside warfare or civil unrest and are carried out by military or paramilitary units. Unlike genocide, a massacre aims to terrorize or eliminate an immediate perceived threat rather than to destroy an entire people — My Lai and El Mozote are the canonical cases in this synopsis.

politicalSlaughter.definition: Large-scale killing by a state or political movement against its own citizens, targeted by political category — class, loyalty, ideology — rather than ethnicity.
politicalSlaughter.extendedDefinition: Sometimes called politicide or democide, political slaughter proceeds through purges, engineered famine, forced labor, and mass execution. The Holodomor and the Cambodian Killing Fields are the exemplar cases; death tolls can equal or exceed those of genocides even though the legal category differs.

ethnicCleansing.definition: The systematic forced removal or extermination of ethnic or religious groups from a given area.
ethnicCleansing.extendedDefinition: A euphemism that entered global vocabulary during the Bosnian War: a deliberate policy designed to remove, by violent and terror-inspiring means, the civilian population of another ethnic or religious group from certain geographic areas. At Srebrenica, international tribunals ruled that ethnic cleansing crossed into genocide.

perpetrator.definition: An individual who carries out, plans, organizes, or facilitates acts of mass violence.
perpetrator.extendedDefinition: In mass atrocity contexts, perpetrators range from direct killers to list-makers, transporters, and propagandists. A central finding of the research summarized here is that most perpetrators are psychiatrically unremarkable — ordinary people transformed by constructed situations.

bystander.definition: Someone who is present at an event or situation but does not take part in it.
bystander.extendedDefinition: In atrocity research, bystanders play crucial roles through action or inaction — from the international community's withdrawal from Rwanda to individual neighbors who hid the hunted. Their responses can enable, resist, or mitigate mass violence.

dehumanization.definition: The psychological process of regarding or treating another person or group as less than human.
dehumanization.extendedDefinition: In mass-violence research, dehumanizing or contaminating representations can reduce moral restraint and make harm easier to justify. Dutton et al. discuss symbolic restructuring of target groups as viral or cancerous, but Ares does not treat dehumanization as a universal stage that every case must pass through.
dehumanization.sourceNote: Process-synthesis context: Dutton, Boyanowsky & Bond (2005), abstract and §10.1, pp. 437, 457–458.

moralDisengagement.definition: The set of psychological maneuvers by which people commit harm while preserving their self-image as decent.
moralDisengagement.extendedDefinition: Albert Bandura's catalogue includes euphemistic labeling ("resettlement," "special treatment"), displacement of responsibility onto authority, diffusion of responsibility across the group, dehumanization of victims, and victim-blaming. Perpetrator testimony across every era reads like a checklist of these mechanisms.

obedienceToAuthority.definition: The willingness of individuals to follow commands from perceived legitimate authorities, even when the commands involve harming others.
obedienceToAuthority.extendedDefinition: Demonstrated experimentally by Stanley Milgram in 1961, when 65% of ordinary volunteers delivered what they believed were maximum-voltage shocks on instruction. Authority does more than compel — it absorbs responsibility, letting each participant locate the decision elsewhere.

groupPolarization.definition: The tendency of groups to adopt positions more extreme than the initial inclinations of their individual members.
groupPolarization.extendedDefinition: In mass-violence settings, perceived threat, in-group conformity and pressure from influential actors can widen social distance and hostility. Dutton et al. discuss polarization as one possible consequence of threat and conformity, not as a required stage in every episode of mass violence.
groupPolarization.sourceNote: Process-synthesis context: Dutton, Boyanowsky & Bond (2005), §10.1, pp. 457–458.

diffusionOfResponsibility.definition: The phenomenon in which individuals feel less personal responsibility for an outcome when responsibility is shared across a group.
diffusionOfResponsibility.extendedDefinition: Mass atrocity divides its labor — list-makers, transporters, cordon troops, shooters, buriers — until each participant holds a fragment too small, in his own eyes, to constitute the crime. A firing squad exists so that no one fired the shot.

situationalTransition.definition: A change in social or immediate conditions that can alter behavior, inhibition, identity or perceived norms in ways that make previously unacceptable violence more possible.
situationalTransition.extendedDefinition: Dutton et al. use transition as a problem to be explained rather than a single ladder. They review several theories and explicitly distinguish long-term shaping and desensitization from short-term transitions under stress, orders and combat conditions. The paper also discusses individual variation, so Ares does not treat transition as automatic or uniform.

escalation.definition: The process by which conflict, coercion or violence increases in intensity, scope or severity over time.
escalation.extendedDefinition: Ares uses escalation descriptively, not as the name of a fixed six- or eight-stage model. The Ares 2.0 process synthesis groups interacting conditions discussed by Dutton et al.; those domains can overlap, recur and reinforce one another rather than forming a universal sequence.
escalation.sourceNote: See the source-mapped Ares process synthesis in Part IV; Dutton, Boyanowsky & Bond (2005), especially §§8–10 and 15–18.

propaganda.definition: Systematic communication designed to shape perception and mobilize action toward a political goal, typically by demonizing a target group.
propaganda.extendedDefinition: In every case studied here, sustained propaganda preceded and accompanied the violence — from Radio RTLM reading out addresses in Rwanda to Ottoman framing of Armenians as an internal enemy. Its function is to dismantle empathy and make participation feel like duty or self-defense.

ideology.definition: A system of ideas and ideals forming the basis of political theory, policy, and justification.
ideology.extendedDefinition: Ideologies provide the explanatory frame that legitimizes targeting specific groups — racial purity, class war, national security. They convert killing from crime into program: something with a rationale, a vocabulary, and a promised future.

impunity.definition: Exemption from punishment or accountability for crimes committed.
impunity.extendedDefinition: Expected impunity is a precondition of mass violence — perpetrators act because they believe no consequence will follow — and post-atrocity impunity seeds the next round. The tribunals for Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia were built explicitly to break this expectation.

denial.definition: The organized rejection, minimization, concealment or reframing of an atrocity by perpetrators, institutions or successors.
denial.extendedDefinition: Denial and obfuscation appear in the historical cases discussed by Dutton et al., but the paper does not establish denial as the final stage of an Ares/Dutton process model. Ares therefore treats denial as a historical and accountability phenomenon rather than as a required terminal node in the Part IV synthesis.
denial.sourceNote: Dutton, Boyanowsky & Bond (2005) discuss case-specific denial and obfuscation; Ares does not import Stanton's terminal-stage framing into its Dutton-based synthesis.

forensicEthology.definition: The proposed empirical study of human collective violence using the methods ethologists apply to animal behavior — triggers, thresholds, and recurring behavioral sequences.
forensicEthology.extendedDefinition: Advanced in the authors' broader work, forensic ethology treats massacres as leaving behavioral signatures that can be catalogued and compared across cases — the rage of a unit that has taken casualties from an invisible enemy, the crowd dynamics of a militia at a roadblock — with the goal of anticipation rather than only explanation.

atrocity.definition: An act of extreme cruelty or violence, typically against defenseless victims.
atrocity.extendedDefinition: In international usage, "mass atrocity" is the collective term for genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, and ethnic cleansing — the four crimes named in the UN's Responsibility to Protect framework.
